## Question 1: Compare KNN and logistic regression

Use [breast-cancer.csv](data/breast-cancer.csv), which contains 569 cases from the [Wisconsin Diagnostic Breast Cancer dataset](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/17/breast%2Bcancer%2Bwisconsin%2Bdiagnostic). Predict `y` (1 for malignant and 0 for benign) using `mean_radius`, `mean_texture`, and `mean_smoothness`.

Set a random seed and randomly split the observations into 70% training and 30% test data. Use the same split for every model. Standardize the predictors using the training means and standard deviations, and apply the same transformations to the test data.

Fit ordinary logistic regression with an intercept and no penalty, and KNN with Euclidean distance, equal neighbor weights, and

$$k\in\{5,15,25,35,45\}.$$

Using the estimated probabilities for `y = 1` on the test data, plot all six ROC curves in one figure and report their AUC values. Which of the six fitted models do you prefer? Give a brief justification based on your results.

```{r, message = FALSE}
set.seed(43201)

# Read .csv file and randomly split observations into 70% training and 30% test data
# Source: https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/r-language/split-the-dataset-into-the-training-test-set-in-r/
df_breast_cancer <- read.csv("data/breast-cancer.csv")

n <- nrow(df_breast_cancer)
sample_index <- sample(seq_len(n), size = floor(0.70 * n))

train <- df_breast_cancer[sample_index, ]
test <- df_breast_cancer[-sample_index, ]

# Standardize the predictors using training means and standard deviations
predictors <- c("mean_radius", "mean_texture", "mean_smoothness")

train_mean <- colMeans(train[predictors])
train_sd <- sapply(train[predictors], sd)

X_train <- train
X_train[predictors] <- scale(train[predictors],
                             center = train_mean,
                             scale = train_sd)
y_train <- train$y

# Apply the same transformations to the test data
X_test <- test
X_test[predictors] <- scale(test[predictors],
                            center = train_mean,
                            scale = train_sd)
y_test <- test$y

# Fit ordinary logistic regression w/ an intercept and no penalty
# Source: https://teazrq.github.io/stat432rpy/topics/classification-evaluation/classification-model-evaluation.html
log_fit <- glm(y ~ ., data = X_train, family = binomial())
log_prob <- predict(log_fit, newdata = X_test, type = "response")

# Fit KNN with Euclidean distance, equal neighbor weights, and k_values
# Source: https://teazrq.github.io/stat432rpy/topics/nearest-neighbors/knn-and-local-averaging.html
library(kknn)

k_values <- seq(from = 5, to = 45, by = 10)
knn_probs <- list()

for (i in seq_along(k_values)){
  knn_fit <- kknn(y ~ ., train = X_train, test = X_test, 
                  k = k_values[i], kernel = "rectangular")
  
  knn_probs[[i]] <- as.vector(fitted(knn_fit))
}

# Convert knn_probs from list to a dataframe for readability
df_knn_probs <- as.data.frame(knn_probs)
names(df_knn_probs) <- paste0("k", k_values)

# Combine knn_probs and log_prob
df_knn_log_probs <- cbind(log_prob, df_knn_probs)

# Use estimated probabilities for y = 1 on test data
library(pROC)

roc_list <- list()
auc_values <- c()

for (m in names(df_knn_log_probs)){
  roc_list[[m]] <- roc(y_test, df_knn_log_probs[[m]], quiet = TRUE)
  auc_values[[m]] <- auc(roc_list[[m]])
}

# Plot all six ROC curves in one figure
plot(roc_list[[1]], type = "l", col = "deepskyblue", lwd = 3,
     main = "ROC curves for logistic regression and KNN")
lines(roc_list[[2]], type = "l", col = "darkorange", lwd = 3)
lines(roc_list[[3]], type = "l", col = "darkred", lwd = 3)
lines(roc_list[[4]], type = "l", col = "forestgreen", lwd = 3)
lines(roc_list[[5]], type = "l", col = "darkorchid", lwd = 3)
lines(roc_list[[6]], type = "l", col = "black", lwd = 3)

legend("bottomright",
       legend = paste(names(roc_list), sprintf("AUC = %.3f", auc_values)),
       col = c("deepskyblue", "darkorange", 
               "darkred", "forestgreen", 
               "darkorchid", "black"),
       lwd = 2,
       bty = "n"
       )

auc_values
```

From Week 6 Lecture: Evaluating Classification Models, "\[t\]he area under the ROC curve, or AUC, summarizes how well the fitted probabilities rank the two classes. It ranges from zero to one." I prefer the logistic regression model because it has the highest test AUC of 0.989. The logistic regression AUC is very close to 1, which means "almost every positive case is ranked above every negative case".

## Question 2: Training and test ROC curves

Use the same data, training/test split, and standardization as in Question 1. Fit KNN with Euclidean distance, equal neighbor weights, and

$$k\in\{1,3,5,10,20\}.$$

Use each fitted model to estimate probabilities for both the training and test observations. For training predictions, include each observation itself among its $k$ nearest neighbors.

For each $k$, use a separate panel to show the training and test ROC curves together. Report both AUC values.

Explain the difference between training and test performance and how it changes with $k$. In particular, explain what happens at $k=1$ and why training performance may not reflect performance on new observations.

```{r}
# Fit KNN with Euclidean distance, equal neighbor weights, and k_values2
k_values2 <- c(1, 3, 5, 10, 20)

train_probs <- list()
test_probs <- list()

roc_train <- list()
roc_test <- list()

auc_train <- c()
auc_test <- c()

for (i in seq_along(k_values2)){
  knn_fit_train <- kknn(y ~ ., train = X_train, test = X_train, 
                  k = k_values2[i], kernel = "rectangular")
  
  knn_fit_test <- kknn(y ~ ., train = X_train, test = X_test, 
                        k = k_values2[i], kernel = "rectangular")
  
  # Use each fitted model to estimate probailities for both the training and test observations
  train_probs <- as.vector(fitted(knn_fit_train))
  test_probs <- as.vector(fitted(knn_fit_test))
  
  # For each k, compute ROC and AUC values
  roc_train[[i]] <- roc(y_train, train_probs, quiet = TRUE)
  roc_test[[i]] <- roc(y_test, test_probs, quiet = TRUE)
  
  auc_train[i] <- auc(roc_train[[i]])
  auc_test[i] <- auc(roc_test[[i]])
  
}

# For each k, use a separate panel to show the training and test ROC curves together. Report both AUC values.
# k = 1
plot(roc_train[[1]], type = "l", col = "deepskyblue", lwd = 3,
     main = "Train and Test ROC curves for k = 1")
lines(roc_test[[1]], type = "l", col = "darkorange", lwd = 3)
legend("bottomright",
       legend = c("Train ROC", "Test ROC"),
       col = c("deepskyblue", "darkorange"),
       lwd = 2,
       bty = "n"
)

# k = 3
plot(roc_train[[2]], type = "l", col = "deepskyblue", lwd = 3,
     main = "Train and Test ROC curves for k = 3")
lines(roc_test[[2]], type = "l", col = "darkorange", lwd = 3)
legend("bottomright",
       legend = c("Train ROC", "Test ROC"),
       col = c("deepskyblue", "darkorange"),
       lwd = 2,
       bty = "n"
)

# k = 5
plot(roc_train[[3]], type = "l", col = "deepskyblue", lwd = 3,
     main = "Train and Test ROC curves for k = 5")
lines(roc_test[[3]], type = "l", col = "darkorange", lwd = 3)
legend("bottomright",
       legend = c("Train ROC", "Test ROC"),
       col = c("deepskyblue", "darkorange"),
       lwd = 2,
       bty = "n"
)

# k = 10
plot(roc_train[[4]], type = "l", col = "deepskyblue", lwd = 3,
     main = "Train and Test ROC curves for k = 10")
lines(roc_test[[4]], type = "l", col = "darkorange", lwd = 3)
legend("bottomright",
       legend = c("Train ROC", "Test ROC"),
       col = c("deepskyblue", "darkorange"),
       lwd = 2,
       bty = "n"
)

# k = 20
plot(roc_train[[5]], type = "l", col = "deepskyblue", lwd = 3,
     main = "Train and Test ROC curves for k = 20")
lines(roc_test[[5]], type = "l", col = "darkorange", lwd = 3)
legend("bottomright",
       legend = c("Train ROC", "Test ROC"),
       col = c("deepskyblue", "darkorange"),
       lwd = 2,
       bty = "n"
)

# Report AUC values
auc_results <- data.frame(
  k = k_values2,
  auc_train = auc_train,
  auc_test = auc_test
)
auc_results
```

Training performance is measured using training data whereas testing performance is measured using testing data (data not used to fit the KNN model). As k increases, the train ROC curve becomes smoother and closer to the test ROC curve. However, at k = 10 and k =15, the train ROC curve becomes less smooth and is under the test ROC curve.

At k = 1, the KNN model relies on the closest data point, which makes the model very flexible. The training AUC value is 1 (i.e., a perfect ROC curve), but the testing AUC value is less than 1 due to noisy predictions. In other words, the model overfits on the training data and does not perform well on the testing data.
